w: What's tested Dr. Herr's study guide for this lecture: the common disorders of the vulva, vagina and cervix; telling neoplastic lesions from non-neoplastic ones; the important infectious causes (infectious vaginitis: Candida and Trichomonas; HPV); the relationship between HPV and cervical neoplasia; and the age-related patterns of the tumors (sarcoma botryoides in little girls, squamous cell carcinoma in women of reproductive age, the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma and the aggressive endometrial carcinoma in older women). Key terms: lichen sclerosus, condyloma acuminatum, sarcoma botryoides, HPV, cervical neoplasia, infectious vaginitis The cervix's transformation zone, where the glandular and squamous epithelia meet and "fight": constantly inflamed, open to HPV infection, and where cervical cancer arises; the precursors (low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions), 90 percent linked to HPV, and the koilocyte Lichen sclerosus, where Dr. Dal Zotto paused "because this is important": the one non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinoma, the HPV-independent squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva in older women Lichen planus, "because you're going to be dentists": vulvar and oral lesions together point to it The endometrium's two carcinomas, the leiomyoma (very common, abnormal bleeding), and the breast: ductal versus lobular carcinoma, in situ versus invasive, Paget disease of the nipple, the receptors (estrogen, progesterone, HER2) and gynecomastia What the lecture said you don't need: the details of the new cervical screening (know only that management is now risk-based), the classification of ovarian tumors (know that most are epithelial, and that ovarian cancer is lethal), and how ductal and lobular carcinoma in situ differ under the microscope Dr. Dal Zotto gave Lecture 22 on Wednesday, November 18, after the break that ended Lecture 21 (the recording starts at 2 pm). The deck, "Pathology of Female Reproductive System", goes from the embryology and anatomy of the female genital tract to the cervix, the uterine corpus, the ovary, the vagina and the vulva, and ends with the breast, which isn't part of the genital tract but belongs to the female reproductive system ("it's a gland that derives from the skin"). The lecture finished early. These notes follow the recording. These notes are written from the recording. The slides were posted the same day but couldn't be opened for this update yet, so a detail that is only on a slide (one not read aloud) isn't here. The recording's captions name every speaker "Michael Herr", the room's Zoom account. Where the female genital tract comes from Early in development, beside the mesonephros, a tube arises on each side from the coelomic cavity: the paramesonephric duct. The two ducts fuse at their lower (caudal) ends, and that fusion gives the uterus, the upper third of the vagina and, from the parts that stay separate, the fallopian tubes. The rest of the vagina comes from another structure, derived from the urogenital sinus. The lecture put this "about the first week of gestation" and called the mesonephros "the future kidney". Embryology texts place the paramesonephric ducts at about the sixth week, and the mesonephros is a temporary kidney; the permanent kidney comes from the metanephros. No question here depends on either. The uterus The uterus, vagina and the other female genital organs sit between the bladder in front and the rectum behind. The uterus is a small organ, no more than 10 centimeters long, triangular. Its lower (distal) part is the cervix, its upper (proximal) part the corpus, the body. It connects with the two elongated fallopian tubes, which reach the ovaries, where the female germ cells are. Opened, it has a cavity in the corpus and a canal, the endocervical canal, that connects the corpus with the vagina. From the outside in: the serosa, a lining of pelvic peritoneum; the myometrium, very thick smooth muscle; and the endometrium, a thin glandular mucosa about 1 millimeter thick lining the cavity. The cervix and its transformation zone The endocervix, lining the endocervical canal, is mucinous glandular (columnar) epithelium. The ectocervix, the part you see through the vagina, is squamous epithelium, like the skin but non-keratinizing. Seen through the vagina, the ectocervix is white and the endocervical mucosa is redder, pushing out toward the ectocervix. Where the two epithelia meet is the transformation zone, the junction of the epithelia. Through the reproductive years the glandular epithelium of the endocervix tries to grow out onto the ectocervix and the squamous epithelium tries to grow into the canal: they collide, "what we call the fighting of epithelia." So the transformation zone is constantly inflamed and injured, and that chronic inflammation makes it susceptible to infection, above all HPV, the virus that affects the whole genital tract in women and men. That is why the transformation zone is where cervical cancer arises. Cervical cancer and screening Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide; breast cancer is first. It is less frequent in the United States because screening (Papanicolaou cytology, the Pap test) finds the premalignant lesions early and is well established and widespread. Still, about a fourth of U.S. women can't get or don't have access to screening, and the lecture said cervical cancer will develop in about 5 percent of those not screened correctly. Effective screening reduces both the incidence and the mortality significantly. The HPV vaccine is very good at reducing the incidence of cervical cancer, especially when adolescents are vaccinated; but it may take decades, until those women reach their 40s and 50s, to see its full benefit, and some uninsured women can't get even a simple screening or the vaccine. Cervical screening has changed in the past 5 years: management is now based on each patient's risk of a high-grade lesion (CIN3), calculated patient by patient. The lecture's example: above about a 4 percent risk the clinician treats; below it, surveillance. The slide's details aren't needed ("you can skip it"); know only that the management is now risk-based. The precursors: squamous intraepithelial lesions The precursors of cervical cancer are squamous intraepithelial lesions (SIL; also called cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN), because they affect the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix, as penile intraepithelial lesions do on the penis. They are low grade (LSIL), which progress slowly and can regress, or high grade (HSIL), which are less likely to regress and more likely to progress to carcinoma. About 90 percent are linked to HPV, in the reproductive years. HPV's mark on a cell, its cytopathic effect, is the koilocyte: a bigger nucleus with a clear halo around it, a true cavity in the cytoplasm (hence the name, from the Greek for hollow). It is what cytology looks for to say there is a squamous intraepithelial lesion, and it is easy to recognize, in a Pap smear and in a biopsy of the ectocervix. A high-grade lesion is more abnormal: the epithelium shows hyperchromasia, crowding and loss of its normal maturation, and in cytology the cells have less cytoplasm (a higher nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio) and pleomorphic nuclei, of different sizes and shapes. These lesions are in situ, confined to the epithelium, but in time they can invade the stroma and become squamous cell carcinoma. Where Lines the endocervical canal The part seen through the vagina Epithelium Mucinous glandular (columnar) Squamous, non-keratinizing Seen through the vagina Red White The uterine corpus: myometrium and endometrium Most of the corpus wall is smooth muscle, the myometrium. Why so much? It contracts to collapse the vessels and stop the bleeding of each menstrual cycle, month to month, and it pushes the baby out at delivery. The endometrium is a thin glandular mucosa that responds to the ovarian cycle. For about the first 15 days the follicle makes a lot of estrogen, and the endometrium has long, straight glands, parallel to each other and perpendicular to the surface, very orderly: "tubes in a rack." After ovulation progesterone dominates: the glands coil and secrete glycoproteins and other substances to receive an embryo. If there isn't one, the lining is shed around day 28: menstruation. Benign conditions of the endometrium Chronic endometritis, inflammation of the endometrium, is benign and frequent, and one of the most common causes of infertility: a woman trying to get pregnant who looks healthy and has no symptoms. It can also cause abnormal uterine bleeding or pain. The physician samples the endometrium, and the pathologist finds plasma cells in the stroma. It is easily treated with antibiotics, and the patient can then get pregnant. Endometrial polyps are proliferations of the endometrium's glands and stroma. In older patients they can be the source of a carcinoma, so they are usually sampled entirely. Endometrial carcinoma: two types "Just know that there are two types of carcinomas": Endometrioid adenocarcinoma, which looks somewhat like normal endometrium (hence the name): tied to estrogen stimulation, in obese patients with excess estrogen or women taking estrogen without progesterone to counteract it. It is well differentiated and less aggressive, and the patients are usually younger (the lecture said premenopausal or perimenopausal). The other type, in older, postmenopausal women (over 65): it looks nothing like the endometrium, and it is more aggressive, with a worse prognosis. Tumors of the myometrium: leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma The leiomyoma is the benign tumor of the uterine smooth muscle, and it is very frequent: the lecture said nearly every woman has some by perimenopause or after. Leiomyomas are white, elastic, very well-circumscribed nodules in the myometrium. "It's like having a foreign body in the midst of the myometrium": the myometrium can't contract well, so the usual symptom is excess, abnormal uterine bleeding. The malignant one, the leiomyosarcoma, is very aggressive and can metastasize to the lung very easily. Textbooks put leiomyomas mostly in the reproductive years, shrinking after menopause; no question here depends on the age. The ovary The ovary gives rise to a plethora of tumors; the classification isn't needed ("Don't shoot me. I don't need you to know this"). Know that most ovarian tumors come from the surface epithelium (the epithelial tumors); others come from the germ cells (the germ cell tumors, as in the testis) and from the stroma. Ovarian cancer is lethal: it causes more deaths than its frequency would suggest, it is very aggressive, it needs a lot of chemotherapy and debulking surgery, and the prognosis isn't good. The vagina The vagina has non-neoplastic and neoplastic conditions. The most frequent non-neoplastic one is inflammation, vaginitis: "everybody has in their life vaginitis." The neoplastic ones are squamous, because the vagina is lined by squamous epithelium: vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VaIN) and squamous cell carcinoma, which affect women of reproductive age. In very young girls, under 5, a different tumor is prevalent: sarcoma botryoides, an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, a very primitive tumor. It has a good prognosis if it is found in time and treated with surgery and chemotherapy. "So know that there are certain tumors that affect the girls, and usually the squamous cell carcinomas affect the women in reproductive age." Vaginitis Vaginitis is infectious or non-infectious: Candida, a fungus: its pseudohyphae look like "little sticks" in the cytology, with a lot of inflammation; very frequent. Trichomonas vaginalis, a sexually transmitted protozoan, a very common cause of vaginitis: easy to diagnose in cytology, because it looks like a squamous cell but has cytoplasmic prolongations (pseudopods). Atrophic vaginitis, non-infectious, very common in older women, not related to any infectious agent. The vulva The vulva has non-infectious inflammatory disorders and neoplastic disorders. Its infections are many, the same ones that affect the vagina, the cervix and the male genital tract. The three non-infectious inflammatory disorders to know: Lichen simplex chronicus A thickening of the vulvar skin (a squamous mucosa) from continuous scratching and rubbing. In older patients, an atrophic epithelium with less estrogen becomes itchy and the patient scratches; or a psychological problem leads to scratching. The epithelium thickens, with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis and acanthosis, and the skin looks leathery. It is a reaction to many conditions that cause pruritus. Lichen sclerosus "I want to pause here because this is important." Lichen sclerosus has an unknown cause; it is postulated to be autoimmune, but that isn't proven. Most important, it predisposes to premalignant and malignant lesions of the vulva, the squamous cell carcinomas. Some vulvar squamous cell carcinomas are associated with HPV and others aren't; the ones not associated with HPV are associated with lichen sclerosus, in older women. The epithelium is completely atrophic, and the hallmark is extensive dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, pink material in the dermis. The vulva looks very smooth, like parchment paper or cellophane. Lichen sclerosus itches, so the patient scratches, and lichen simplex chronicus can form on top of it. "Lichen sclerosus is the single non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinomas." Lichen planus "You must know about this, because you're going to be dentists." Lichen planus is an inflammatory disorder of the oral mucosa and also of the vulva, where its diagnosis is often delayed because it isn't recognized. If a patient has vulvar and oral lesions, it is most likely lichen planus. It is postulated to be an autoimmune, cell-mediated disorder; it causes erosions, sometimes very painful and ulcerated, in the vulva and the mouth, with many inflammatory cells, especially lymphocytes, in the dermis. The diagnosis is easy: send the biopsy to the pathology laboratory fresh, not in formalin, for immunofluorescence, which shows no immune complexes and a deposit of fibrin. The patient is treated with steroids. Cause Chronic scratching and rubbing (itch from atrophy, or psychological) Unknown; postulated autoimmune Postulated autoimmune, cell-mediated Epithelium Thickened: hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis Completely atrophic Erosions, ulcers Dermis Not stressed Sclerosis and hyalinization (pink) Many lymphocytes Looks Leathery Smooth, like parchment paper or cellophane Painful erosions; often in the mouth too Cancer risk No Yes: HPV-independent squamous cell carcinoma in older women Not stressed Diagnosis and treatment Treat what causes the itch Find it early, before carcinoma develops Fresh biopsy for immunofluorescence; steroids Condyloma acuminatum of the vulva As on the penis, condyloma acuminatum can affect any part of the anogenital tract. It is associated with HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types: a benign condition, though it can be painful or ulcerate. It forms finger-like, exophytic, wart-like (verruciform) lesions, big or small, and under the microscope it shows koilocytes, because it is HPV. Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: two kinds The premalignant squamous intraepithelial lesions lead to squamous cell carcinoma, and, as on the penis, there are two kinds: HPV-associated: from HPV 16 and 18 ("bigger numbers"); a better prognosis, and radiosensitive. HPV-independent: in older women, over 60, associated with lichen sclerosus. That is why lichen sclerosus has to be diagnosed in time and treated, not left until a squamous cell carcinoma develops. Cervix Inflammation of the transformation zone Low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions; squamous cell carcinoma Vagina Vaginitis: Candida, Trichomonas, atrophic Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia, squamous cell carcinoma; sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5 Vulva Lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus; condyloma acuminatum (a benign HPV lesion) Squamous intraepithelial lesions; squamous cell carcinoma (HPV 16 and 18, or lichen sclerosus) Girls under 5 Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) of the vagina Women of reproductive age Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and vagina, HPV-related; endometrioid adenocarcinoma in younger women with excess estrogen Older women HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (over 60, lichen sclerosus); the aggressive endometrial carcinoma (over 65) The breast The breast isn't part of the genital tract but is part of the female reproductive system: a modified skin gland. Before birth it arises from a thickening of the ectoderm that runs on both sides from the armpit to the groin, the milk line. Only the thickenings in front of the pectoralis muscle develop into breasts; the rest regress. But ectopic breast tissue can be found anywhere along the milk line, in the vulva for example, and carcinomas can arise in it too. The breast is made of acini arranged in lobules, which make milk, and ducts, which carry it; the ducts converge on the nipple, where the larger lactiferous ducts let the milk out after delivery. Benign conditions of the breast Mastitis, the most common inflammation, during breastfeeding: skin bacteria enter the lactiferous ducts and inflame the ducts and lobules (an ascending inflammation). Very painful, and easily treated with antibiotics. Duct ectasia: the ducts dilate and can break, leaking their secretions into the tissue, where an inflammatory reaction heals with scarring that can retract the nipple. Traumatic fat necrosis: for example, a seatbelt pushing against the breast in a car accident. Intraductal proliferative and non-proliferative lesions: the proliferative ones carry a little more risk of carcinoma. Breast carcinoma Like any carcinoma, breast carcinoma is in situ or invasive. The carcinomas in situ: ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), from the ducts; lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), from the lobules; and Paget disease of the nipple. The WHO now considers LCIS a benign lesion, neoplastic but benign, and no treatment is needed. DCIS needs treatment, usually surgery, with or without radiotherapy, and it has a good prognosis. (How they differ under the microscope: "you don't need to know that.") Invasive carcinomas are also ductal or lobular. An invasive ductal carcinoma forms little ducts, or glands; an invasive lobular carcinoma typically forms no glands and infiltrates the stroma's collagen in single files. Invasive carcinomas are aggressive, but today breast carcinoma is the carcinoma best cured: with surgery, with or without radiotherapy, and hormonal therapy, many women are cured completely and only need surveillance. Mammary Paget disease is a carcinoma: carcinoma cells involve the epithelium of the nipple, which looks like a scaly, red area. It is usually associated with an in situ or invasive carcinoma in the breast, so whenever it is seen, mammography or other imaging looks for that carcinoma, and the prognosis is the underlying carcinoma's. The prognosis of an invasive breast carcinoma depends on its histologic type (ductal or lobular), its size, the presence of lymph node metastases (the stage), and whether it expresses estrogen or progesterone receptors and the surface protein HER2. All of them can be targeted by specific drugs, so knowing a tumor's receptor and HER2 status guides the treatment: surgical excision, with or without chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and anti-estrogen therapy for a tumor that expresses estrogen receptors. In situ DCIS: needs treatment (surgery, with or without radiotherapy); good prognosis LCIS: neoplastic but benign (WHO); no treatment needed Invasive Forms little ducts or glands No glands; single files infiltrating the stroma The male breast The male breast has the same pathology as the female breast, but its cancer is found later, because men have no mammography or screening: the cancer is so rare that a screening program isn't justified. Much more common is gynecomastia, an enlarged breast from excess estrogen: in obese men, whose fat has the aromatase that converts testosterone to estradiol, and in weightlifters who take testosterone. The lecture called LCIS benign, with no treatment needed, and the questions here follow the lecture. Texts also call it a marker of a higher risk of breast cancer, followed with surveillance.
